name: Isomorphism
tagline: Reversible anonymisation of Swiss personal data for Python. AHV numbers, IBANs, names, addresses, dates of birth and more become placeholders before a model call and come back in the answer, also while it streams.
seoTitle: Isomorphism – anonymise Swiss personal data (AHV, IBAN, names, addresses) for LLMs in Python
description:
Before a text goes to a language model, Isomorphism replaces Swiss personal data with placeholders like [AHV_1], [IBAN_1] and [PERSON_1]. After the answer comes back, restore() puts the real values in again, and Restorer does the same for an answer that arrives in pieces, even when a placeholder is split between two pieces. The same value always gets the same placeholder, so the model can still follow who is meant.

The checksum recognisers know the Swiss formats: AHV numbers (EAN-13), IBANs of Switzerland and Liechtenstein (mod 97), UID numbers (mod 11), cards (Luhn), PostFinance accounts and Swiss phone numbers in their usual spellings. Numbers that look right but fail the check are reported as well, with lower confidence, because a typo in a document is still personal data. Names, companies, addresses and dates of birth are found with patterns, titles, a list of common first names, legal forms and context words, in German, French, Italian and English, and names of authorities such as Steueramt St. Gallen stay in the text. Every hit comes back with kind, position, confidence and recogniser, never the value, so it fits an audit log.

It runs fully local: pure Python 3.12 or newer, no dependencies, no network calls, no telemetry. The mapping with the real values is never logged or stored by the package. Microsoft Presidio can be added as an optional backend for names in running text. The README reports hit rate and false alarms per kind on invented Swiss texts. No tool finds all personal data, so treat it as one protective layer. MIT-licensed.

code.title: anonymize.py
code.snippet:
from isomorphism import Restorer, anonymize, restore

text = "Hr. Keller, AHV 756.1234.5678.97, IBAN CH93 0076 2011 6238 5295 7, Tel. 071 123 45 67"
safe, mapping = anonymize(text)
# '[PERSON_1], AHV [AHV_1], IBAN [IBAN_1], Tel. [PHONE_1]'

answer = call_your_model(safe)   # the model only sees placeholders
print(restore(answer, mapping))  # the real values are back

r = Restorer(mapping)            # for an answer that arrives in pieces
for piece in call_your_model_stream(safe):
    print(r.feed(piece), end="")
print(r.flush())

for f in mapping.findings:       # audit log, without values
    print(f.kind, f.start, f.end, f.confidence, f.detector, f.checksum_ok)

free: anonymize() replaces personal data with placeholders such as [AHV_1], [IBAN_1], [PERSON_1] and [ADDRESS_1]; restore() puts the real values back
The same value gets the same placeholder inside one call, so a model can follow who is meant
Streaming: Restorer and restore_stream restore an answer that arrives in pieces, also when a placeholder is split between two pieces

IBANs of Switzerland and Liechtenstein: mod-97 check, with or without spaces, upper or lower case
UID numbers (CHE): mod-11 check; MWST, TVA, IVA and HR stay in the text
Swiss phone numbers: +41, 0041, +41 (0)71, 071 123 45 67, 071/123 45 67, (071) … and ten bare digits
Email addresses
Persons: after a title (Hr., Frau, Dr., M., Mme, signora …), first name plus surname from a list of about 440 common first names, Muster, Anna, the same surname again later and a first name alone
Companies: the name before AG, GmbH, SA, Sàrl, Sagl, KlG, KG, Ltd, Inc, LLC
Addresses: street with number and postcode with place in German, French, Italian and English, also with CH- before the postcode
Dates of birth: only after context words such as geb., Geburtsdatum, né le, nata il, date of birth, so invoice dates stay untouched
Card numbers with Luhn check and accounts: PostFinance numbers with mod-10 check and digits after Konto, compte, conto or account
Authorities such as Steueramt St. Gallen or Handelsregisteramt Zürich are never replaced; keep=[…] takes exact values or patterns for your own exceptions
Numbers with a wrong check digit are still found, with lower confidence (better too many than too few)
Audit log per hit: kind, position, confidence, recogniser and check result, never the value
restore() tolerates changes by the model: [ahv_1] and [ AHV_1 ] still match, unknown placeholders stay unchanged; a placeholder that already stands in your text is never reused
Optional Presidio backend for names in running text: detectors=[presidio_detector(analyzer)], not a dependency, runs locally
The mapping hides its values in repr() and str(); the package logs and stores nothing; pure Python 3.12+, no dependencies, no network calls, no telemetry
Typed (py.typed), tested on Python 3.12 and 3.13 with invented Swiss texts in German, French, Italian and English, hit rate and false alarms per kind in the README

Names, companies, addresses and dates of birth in German, French, Italian and English

faq.q: Does it find names and addresses?
faq.a: Yes, with limits. Names are found after a title (Hr. Keller), as first name plus surname from a list of about 440 common first names, and again when the surname appears later in the text. Companies are found by legal form, addresses by street words and postcodes. These are heuristics, less certain than the checksum kinds, and they can over-report; check the confidence. For other names in running text you can add Presidio.

faq.q: Does anonymising make my processing compliant with the FADP or GDPR?
faq.a: No. Isomorphism is a technical tool, not legal advice. Recognition is pattern based, the surrounding text can still identify a person, and the mapping itself is personal data. You remain responsible for what you send to a model.

faq.q: Where does the mapping with the real values live?
faq.a: In the object that anonymize() returns, in your process. The package never logs or stores it, and repr() shows only the number of placeholders. If you keep it longer than one request, that is up to you; dict(mapping) gives a plain dictionary.

faq.q: What happens with a number that has a typo?
faq.a: It is reported with lower confidence (for example 0.60 instead of 0.99 for an AHV number) and checksum_ok set to False. It is replaced like any other hit, because a mistyped AHV number is still personal data.

faq.q: Does the model give the placeholders back unchanged?
faq.a: Square brackets, capital letters and a number are chosen so models usually return them as they are. restore() also accepts a changed case or spaces inside the brackets, and leaves placeholders that are not in the mapping untouched.

faq.q: How do I restore a streamed answer?
faq.a: Create a Restorer(mapping), call feed(piece) for each piece and flush() at the end, or use restore_stream(pieces, mapping). The end of a piece that could be the start of a placeholder is held back until the next piece, so a placeholder split in two is restored. The demo shows it step by step.

No. Names such as Steueramt St. Gallen, Handelsregisteramt Zürich or Bundesamt für Statistik are left in the text by default (protect_authorities=True). For your own exceptions pass keep=[…] with exact values or compiled patterns.

faq.q: Does it send anything over the network?
faq.a: No. There are no dependencies and no network code. The live demo runs the same package in your browser through Pyodide; the page downloads the Python runtime once from jsDelivr.
Not at the moment. The core is MIT-licensed and contains everything above.
